title: Chef's tapas menu: cloud memory sold in exact portions
idea: Instead of fixed 'set menus' of 4 or 8 GB per vCPU, clouds sell memory on its own in 1 GB increments backed by pooled CXL DIMMs, with pricing that rewards right-sizing. Schedulers bin-pack against measured working-set telemetry rather than requested size.
why: Doing DRAM's job with less: fixed memory-to-vCPU ratios strand ~20-30% of purchased DRAM; a la carte sizing could cut fleet DRAM demand ~15%.

title: Magnify cumulative volume: solarize memory with one open SKU
idea: Define one open-standard memory brick (fixed interface, form factor, capacity) and pay a declining per-GB feed-in subsidy for 10 years that steps down with each doubling of cumulative output, like German PV feed-in tariffs, forcing ~7 volume doublings on cheap processes.
why: Solar fell ~100x per watt through standardization plus guaranteed, declining support; a ~25-30% learning rate over ~7 doublings on a radical low-cost process yields ~100x.

title: Shortage-triggered compulsory licensing of DRAM patents
idea: Po: patents sleep during a shortage. When an official DRAM price index exceeds a threshold (e.g., 2x its 3-year average), any qualified domestic producer may practice listed DRAM patents at a tribunal-set royalty, using government-use and march-in style powers.
why: Removes the litigation risk that deters entrants exactly when entry is most needed; attacks supplier diversity and U.S. manufacturability.

title: Stranded-RAM spot exchange: servers lend idle memory to neighbors
idea: Rearrange who holds memory from fixed owner to live market: a rack broker auctions each server's idle DRAM to neighboring servers every few seconds over CXL 3.x switching or RDMA. A preemption contract lets lenders reclaim their memory within milliseconds.
why: Servers are provisioned for peak memory. A liquid market inside the fleet lets 10-25% fewer DIMMs serve the same workloads.

title: Audio-RAM for AI: approximate grade from row-failed dies
idea: In the 1990s partly defective DRAMs were sold as audio RAM for answering machines, until flash ended that market. Fix: create a formal approximate grade whose bad-row maps ship in the module's SPD, and use these dies for error-tolerant AI data (activations, low-order KV-cache bits, embeddings), with the framework placing critical data only on clean rows.
why: Yield: recovers perhaps 3-8% of wafer output that is now scrapped or deeply discounted, a large number of bits in a shortage.

title: Etch-free printed oxide micro-fab using inkjet and laser sintering
idea: Fuse inkjet or electrohydrodynamic printing of In-Zn-O precursor inks with flash or laser sintering to build gain-cell memory tiles additively. Nothing is etched, so there is no fluorine and no masks, in containerized micro-fabs near customers.
why: Distributed, near-zero-capex (about $5M per pod) supply of low-density working memory for edge and defense, with no PFAS or EUV.

title: Open DRAM multi-project wafer shuttle service
idea: Box[Owner=national lab + incumbent fab x Fab=quarterly MPW runs of DRAM process x Finance=subsidized per-slot pricing]: like MOSIS for memory, startups and universities buy slots on real DRAM front-end flows to test new cells, capacitors and access devices.
why: Innovation rate: cuts the cost of a DRAM test chip from ~$10M+ to ~$100k, speeding new cell concepts to market.

title: Microsecond memory exchange auctions stranded DRAM across tenants
idea: Measured cloud DRAM utilization averages ~50% because memory is provisioned per server for peak. A rack-scale CXL switch runs a continuous double auction that leases 256 MB segments between hosts with microsecond reassignment and hardware isolation, so idle bits are sold rather than stranded.
why: Usable supply: raising effective utilization from ~50% to ~75% is equivalent to ~50% more usable DRAM with zero new wafers.

title: Digital-press maskless lithography with U.S. multi-column e-beam
idea: Adapted from digital presses that killed printing plates for short runs: pattern DRAM's non-periodic layers (periphery, contacts, cut layers) with U.S.-developed multi-column e-beam direct write using hundreds of parallel columns, with no masks and no EUV.
why: Removes mask sets ($10-20M+ per node) and EUV for those layers; suits low-volume U.S. micro-fabs and fast design turns. Throughput limits its use to a few layers (masks, capital, U.S. manufacturability).

title: Nanoimprint stamps for DRAM array layers, DUV for periphery
idea: Po: masks are rubber stamps. The highly periodic array layers (active, buried wordline, bitline, storage-node contact) are patterned by jet-and-flash nanoimprint from e-beam-written master templates, while irregular periphery stays on ArF immersion with mix-and-match alignment.
why: Imprint tools cost a fraction of EUV and use ~10x less power; array redundancy absorbs NIL's isolated defects; attacks capital intensity and energy.

title: Strip-and-rewrite photomask blanks with plasma etch-stop layers
idea: Periphery masks put the absorber over a thin Ru etch-stop on low-expansion quartz; obsolete or damaged masks are stripped selectively in Cl/O2 plasma, re-coated and rewritten, reusing the costly blank many times.
why: Mask blanks come from few suppliers and mask sets cost millions; reuse lowers that barrier and quartz demand.

title: Print-on-demand memory: maskless multibeam runs for niche DRAM SKUs
idea: Print-on-demand publishing killed minimum print runs. Write only the product-specific layers (periphery options, fuses, metal personalization) of automotive, defense and legacy DRAM SKUs with maskless multibeam e-beam, so 1000-wafer lots need no mask set. This moves the long tail off mainstream lines.
why: Masks, capital and supply mix: removes $5-15M mask sets for long-tail SKUs, frees mainstream capacity, and enables trusted U.S. legacy DRAM.

title: Fab-starved memory startups: 180 nm memory-device MPW shuttle
idea: Memory startups (Unity Semiconductor, Spin Memory, Crossbar and others) spent much of their capital just getting wafers made. Fix: a MOSIS-style multi-project wafer service on a 180 nm, 200 mm line with open back-end memory-module slots (capacitor, ferroelectric, resistive, molecular layers), where startups pay per die site and share masks, getting silicon in ~8 weeks for ~$20k.
why: Cuts the cost of a new memory concept's first silicon ~100x and speeds iteration, raising the odds that a new DRAM-class cell reaches volume.

title: No proprietary IP: open DRAM design kit for trench foundries
idea: Self-imposed limit: everything must be open. A consortium releases an open-licensed DRAM macro kit (trench or stacked cell, sense amp, redundancy, DDR/CXL PHY RTL) qualified on foundry processes that already have deep-trench capacitors, so any logic foundry can make commodity-interface DRAM.
why: Breaks the three-maker oligopoly and the IP barrier; adds foundry capacity to DRAM supply. Density is lower, but U.S. manufacturability improves.

title: Vaccine-style advance market commitment for new DRAM entrants
idea: A vaccine primes immune memory before the pathogen arrives. Hyperscalers and government sign a binding advance purchase at a guaranteed price floor for the first N exabits from any qualified new U.S. DRAM entrant, priming capacity years before the next shortage.
why: Removes the demand risk that blocks $15B fab financing; could cut entrants' cost of capital by several hundred bp and pull in 1-2 new fabs (U.S. manufacturability).

title: Vaccine-style advance market commitment for refresh-free 125 C memory
idea: Like the pneumococcal vaccine AMC, governments and automakers pre-commit to buy 100M units at a fixed price from whoever first delivers byte-addressable memory meeting <100 ns access, no refresh at 125 C, and 10-year life.
why: Pulls private capital into a hard technology by guaranteeing demand, targeting the refresh/leakage wall at its worst case (125 C).

title: Sell the broken rows: defect-mapped DRAM with SPD failure maps
idea: Reverse the yield funnel: dies that fail on-chip row/column repair are not scrapped. They ship with a signed bad-row map in the module SPD or CXL device, and the OS/hypervisor retires those pages at boot (badram/memmap style). They sell at a discount as a 'mapped grade' for cloud capacity tiers.
why: Turns scrap into supply: usable bits per wafer rise ~3-8% with almost no capex, at a time when every extra wafer costs a fortune.

title: Ship imperfect dies with a standardized bad-row map
idea: Po: every chip is broken. A JEDEC-style 'fault map in SPD' lets fabs ship dies with up to ~0.5% bad rows beyond on-die repair; BIOS/OS reads the map at boot and retires those physical pages, so dies now downgraded or scrapped become full-price product.
why: Raises good-die yield at leading nodes by an estimated 3-10%, i.e., free wafer capacity; attacks cost per bit and capital intensity.

title: Eliminate the scrap bin: JEDEC bank-disable map for partial-good dies
idea: Eliminate binary pass/fail dies: a JEDEC-standard on-die fuse map records disabled banks/subarrays, and memory controllers plus the OS allocate around them, so a die with one dead bank ships as a 7/8-capacity part instead of being crushed or sold grey.
why: Unrepairable clustered defects cost ~2-6% of wafer bits; harvesting them is like adding a mid-size fab's output at zero capex.

title: Laser shockwave cleaning: plasma pops particles off dry
idea: Replace liquid particle removal with laser-induced plasma shockwaves fired just above the wafer, which knock particles off without contact while local gas suction carries them away. It is used after etch and deposition steps where a rinse is now the default.
why: Dry, chemical-free particle removal cuts the rinse water on those steps >10x. The risk is damage to fragile high-aspect-ratio structures.

title: Chemist's electron sponges: polyoxometalate molecules as 2-bit storage nodes
idea: A chemist sees molecules that soak up electrons like sponges. Graft polyoxometalate clusters (~1 nm, reversibly holding 0-3 extra electrons at distinct potentials) as the storage node on the gate of a vertical oxide-semiconductor read transistor, so one molecule stores 2 bits with no capacitor. U.S. specialty-chemical makers supply self-limiting monolayer inks.
why: Meets the 10x constraint: no capacitor plus 2 bits per cell lets a 4F^2 vertical cell in 3 tiers reach ~9-12x bits/mm^2 at about today's wafer cost. Electron transfer is fast, but retention and stability at 85 C are unproven.

title: Epigenetic binning: deploy sub-spec dies with workload-matched refresh
idea: One genome is expressed differently in different environments. Dies that fail retention or speed bins go to workloads that tolerate them, such as AI inference caches, with per-row retention profiling and controller-managed higher refresh, instead of being scrapped.
why: Raises effective yield by a few % to ~10%, adding bits at zero wafer cost.

title: Revive deep-trench eDRAM as standalone memory chiplets
idea: Po: the logic foundry already makes DRAM. Deep-trench capacitor eDRAM, proven on 32-14 nm SOI logic lines without EUV, is turned into standalone 4-8 Gb capacity chiplets with simplified periphery, built on existing U.S. logic lines and sold via CXL or UCIe.
why: Taps idle mature U.S. logic capacity for DRAM-class memory; ~10+ fF trench caps extend retention; attacks U.S. manufacturability and supplier diversity at some density penalty.

title: Coral-polyp fab growing bay by bay from revenue
idea: Coral reefs grow one self-sufficient polyp at a time. A DRAM fab is built from sealed cleanroom pods, each with its own mini-environment, utilities and material handling; the first pods make legacy parts and each quarter's revenue funds the next pod, so capacity accretes without $15B upfront.
why: ~10x less capital at risk at start; first wafers in ~18 months; capacity tracks demand (capital intensity).

title: Water flows backwards: cascade from final rinse to dirtiest uses
idea: Reverse the plant flow: instead of every tool drawing UPW and draining it, effluent is separated by purity and cascaded. Last-rinse water feeds first rinses, then scrubbers, then cooling makeup, with high-recovery RO/EDI polishing only the tail.
why: With 90%+ reuse, net intake per wafer drops ~10x. That opens water-stressed U.S. sites to new memory fabs.

title: Eliminate the silicon wafer: memory tiles on idle display-glass lines
idea: Eliminate the 300mm wafer and the DRAM fab: retool overbuilt Gen-6/8 LCD/OLED backplane lines (oxide-TFT tools already installed) to build 8-16 stacked tiers of low-temperature oxide-TFT gain-cell arrays on glass, diced into cheap capacity tiles for CXL far memory.
why: Panel area costs ~100x less per cm2 than 300mm silicon and lines are depreciated; with tier stacking, capacity-tier cost per bit could approach DRAM with almost no new capex and no EUV.

title: Internal memory stranding market with CXL pools and spot pricing
idea: Fuse CXL memory pooling with an internal spot market. Each server reports unallocated DRAM (often 25-50% stranded), a broker prices it per GB-minute, and the CXL fabric lends it to hungry VMs, with no change visible to tenants.
why: Raises fleet memory utilization from about 50-60% to 80%+. That works out to 20-30% more usable supply from bits already bought.

title: Shipping-container standard footprint for hot automotive memory
idea: Like the ISO container that made all ships and cranes interchangeable, automakers adopt one solder-down memory footprint, pinout and 125 C/10-year thermal profile for all ECUs, so any qualified supplier's parts drop in without board redesign.
why: Makes automotive memory fungible across vendors and programs, so shortages at one supplier no longer halt car lines (as in 2021).

title: TSMC-for-memory pure-play DRAM foundry with open shuttles
idea: Copy the logic-foundry model that unlocked fabless design: a DRAM-only foundry publishes a cell-array PDK and runs multi-project shuttles so startups can tape out custom periphery, HBM base dies and domain-specific DRAM without owning a fab.
why: Breaks the 3-firm design monopoly; adds design diversity and new demand-specific products, and lets a U.S. fab sell capacity to many customers, raising utilization 10-20 points.

title: Helium-as-a-service recapture skids owned by gas suppliers
idea: Ideal: helium never leaves the fab. Closest achievable: the gas supplier installs and owns cryogenic helium recovery and purification on EUV, etch backside-cooling and leak-test exhausts, and bills per liter avoided, so the fab pays no capex.
why: Helium chokepoint (Qatar offline): 70-90% reuse insulates DRAM output from supply loss.

title: Deposit-only patterning: area-selective ALD with chlorine silicon etch
idea: Fuse area-selective ALD (inhibitor SAMs that block growth on the masked areas) with HBr/Cl2 silicon etch, so dielectrics are only ever grown where wanted and never etched. That removes every CF4/C4F8/NF3 oxide-etch and chamber-clean step from the DRAM flow.
why: Removes fluorinated etch gases (and their supply and regulatory risk) and cuts the number of etch tools, a large share of DRAM capex.

title: Junkyard: harvest retired-phone LPDDR into CXL inference memory modules
idea: Random stimulus 'junkyard' -> phones are memory scrap heaps. Automated desoldering lines at e-waste recyclers pull LPDDR4X/5 packages from ~0.5-1B retired phones a year, test and reball them onto carrier boards behind a CXL controller as KV-cache/far-memory for inference racks.
why: Raises usable supply with near-zero fab capex: ~700M phones x 6 GB x 30% recovered x 80% pass is roughly 1 EB/yr, a few % of world DRAM bits, and it is US-local scarce-resource-free supply.

title: Toyota RESCUE-style multi-tier chokepoint map with prequalified alternates
idea: Adapted from Toyota's post-2011 supplier database tracing parts to tier-N: map every DRAM input down to the mine or plant (quartz, tungsten, neon, resist monomers, helium), flag single-site nodes, and pay to dual-qualify alternates before a crisis.
why: Turns months-long disruptions (helium outage, Spruce Pine hurricane) into weeks; protects the ~5-15% of yearly output exposed to single-node events (scarce resources, supply).

title: Sinclair Half-Good Chips: Sell Partial-Capacity DRAM Die With Fuse Maps
idea: Revive the 1982 ZX Spectrum trick of shipping TI 4532 'half-good' 64K chips: dies that exhaust their repair fuses in one bank-half are fused to a clean half-capacity address map and sold as standard 12/24 Gb SKUs for edge, IoT, consoles and appliances, with a JEDEC 'partial-good' mode register so controllers need no special handling.
why: Cost per bit and supply: recovers dies currently scrapped after redundancy exhaustion (several % of gross dies, more during early node ramps), ~3-8% more sellable bits per wafer and full dies freed for servers.

title: Color change: one-mask optical grating ID enables automated reclaim grading
idea: TRIZ #32 Color change: one mask patterns a diffractive grating code in the top metal readable through the package by IR spectroscopy, carrying lot, bin and retention data so reclaimed dies are auto-sorted and priced without retest.
why: Reuse market friction: cheap trusted provenance lifts reclaimed DRAM yields and buyer confidence.

title: Another dimension: embedded-die PCB DIMMs doubling module density
idea: TRIZ #17 Another dimension: bare DRAM dies are embedded inside the module PCB core and connected with one added laser/litho via layer, while the surfaces carry more packaged dies, doubling GB per DIMM slot.
why: Slot-limited server capacity: more memory per socket without new dies or a new die node.

title: Airbus-style allied DRAM company with stage-hosting by member nations
idea: Po: the factory belongs to many nations. Allied governments (e.g., U.S., Japan, EU, India) co-own one DRAM company in which each hosts a stage (front-end fab, test, packaging, stacking) and receives allocation proportional to equity, Airbus-style.
why: Splits the $15B+ fab ticket across sponsors and creates a fourth supplier outside today's three; attacks capital intensity and chokepoint concentration.

title: Wafer-level burn-in revived with 1990s-made full-wafer contactors
idea: Full-wafer DRAM burn-in (tried in the 1990s-2000s, e.g. Aehr's WaferPak) stalled because full-wafer contactors were costly. Make the contactors with 1990s tools: MEMS spring-probe arrays and polyimide flex membranes patterned at 1-5 um on old 200 mm lines, so every HBM core-die wafer is burned in and screened before stacking.
why: HBM yield is down 20-30% partly because weak dies get stacked; wafer-level screening raises stack yield and relieves test-floor capacity, a bottleneck alongside TSVs.

title: Seeded crystal growth: rapid-melt single-crystal tiers for stacked DRAM
idea: Deposit amorphous SiGe/Ge stripes over oxide, with seed windows opened to the crystalline substrate. Encapsulate them and flash-melt by RTA or pulsed laser so single-crystal growth runs laterally from each seed, as a seed crystal grows a boule. Repeat to stack crystalline lateral access-transistor tiers for 3D DRAM.
why: 3D DRAM lateral-transistor blocker: single-crystal tiers without $50M epi-superlattice tools or wafer bonding. PECVD, RTA and lasers are nanofab-available.

title: Multi-recharge Czochralski: five ingots per quartz crucible
idea: Ideal: a crucible that lasts forever. Closest achievable with existing pullers: retrofit continuous polysilicon recharge feeders and barium-doped devitrification coatings so one crucible yields 4-5 ingots instead of 1-2, with a synthetic sol-gel silica inner liner made from domestic silica.
why: Spruce Pine quartz chokepoint: ~60% less high-purity quartz per wafer.

title: Pyroelectric crystal emitters power cheap multi-beam lithography in micro-fabs
idea: Thermally cycled LiTaO3 crystals build >100 kV/cm surface fields that field-emit electrons without high-voltage supplies. Tile thousands of gated micro-pyro emitters into a maskless multi-beam writer for DRAM periphery layers and low-volume masks.
why: Removes $5-15M mask sets and EUV for low-volume periphery, letting small fabs write custom memory.

title: DRAM-lean label: certification that weans devices off unneeded DRAM
idea: Modeled on Energy Star, a 'DRAM-lean' label for TVs, set-top boxes, routers and car head units certifies firmware that meets a RAM budget (zram, execute-in-place from NOR, pruned services), backed by procurement preferences, returning gigabytes per device to the market.
why: Embedded consumer devices absorb many bits at low utilization; a 30% trim frees meaningful supply.

title: Turnkey EUV-free DRAM fab franchise
idea: Po: a fab is a burger franchise. A franchisor packages a frozen EUV-free DRAM process (DUV plus self-aligned patterning), tool list, recipes, yield-learning database, training academy and a qualification brand; regional franchisees (states, sovereign funds, consortia) build identical fabs and pay royalties per wafer.
why: Copy-exactly replication shrinks yield ramp from years to months and lets capacity grow in parallel without EUV allocation; attacks capital, time and U.S. manufacturability.

title: Benetton dye-later: one universal die configured at packaging
idea: Benetton knits undyed sweaters and dyes them once demand is known. Design a universal DRAM die with fuse-selectable interface (LPDDR5X, DDR5, GDDR-like or HBM-core mode) and organization. Die banks hold unpackaged wafers and commit each one to a SKU only at packaging, against live orders.
why: Usable supply: removes the ~10-20% mix-mismatch loss and the ~3-month product lag, so a shortage in one SKU no longer coexists with a glut in another.

title: Layer offload: non-critical DRAM layers exposed on KrF/i-line elsewhere
idea: Ideal: precious scanners print only the hardest layers. Closest achievable with no new fab: of ~40-60 mask layers, the ~25 coarse ones (implants, pads, upper metals) move to depreciated KrF/i-line scanners in a nearby trailing fab under a wafer-shuttle and overlay-matching protocol.
why: Frees ~30-40% of ArFi scanner time at the constraint tool, so more wafer starts.

title: Cryo-salvage: retention-reject dies run refresh-free in 77 K pods
idea: Worse: scrap dies that fail retention at 85 C. Flip: route them into liquid-nitrogen memory pods where junction and subthreshold leakage collapse by many orders, so cells hold data for days and refresh is switched off entirely.
why: Zero refresh power; turns a few percent of scrap output into supply, with cooling cost amortized over large pooled memory.

title: Eliminate the cleanroom for R&D: glovebox micro-line for oxide-TFT memory
idea: Eliminate the cleanroom for prototyping: a ~$700k line of nitrogen gloveboxes with sputter, ALD and maskless laser direct-write on 100mm glass builds low-temperature oxide-TFT 2T0C arrays to prove yield per dollar within 24 months.
why: Proves capital-light memory manufacturing at ~1/1000 of fab capex before scaling.

title: Eliminate royalty fear: expired-patent freedom-to-operate atlas for legacy DRAM
idea: Eliminate the belief that DRAM is a legal minefield: a ~$400k legal-engineering project maps expired pre-2006 DRAM patents onto a complete 50-90nm stacked-capacitor process and periphery, publishing an open freedom-to-operate atlas and reference flow.
why: Cuts legal cost for any legacy-node entrant from millions to near zero, enabling US micro-fabs and foundries.

title: Generic DRAM: off-patent process reference flow for new entrants
idea: Box[IP=expired 20-30 nm-class 6F2 buried-channel array patents x Owner=open IP pool x Fab=DUV-only reference flow x Business=licensable recipe kit]: assemble a fully off-patent DRAM process and design kit, like generic drugs, so new fabs can make commodity DDR-class parts with no license negotiations.
why: Capital and entry barriers: new entrants skip years of IP risk; legacy-density bits on depreciated tools.

title: Eliminate soldered-equals-scrap: robotic LPDDR harvesting from e-waste boards
idea: Eliminate shredding of phones and laptops with soldered LPDDR: vision-guided robots locally reflow, lift, clean and reball LPDDR packages, test them on socketed ATE, and sell graded parts to low-cost tablet, IoT and SBC makers.
why: LPDDR is roughly a third of DRAM bits and nearly all of it is shredded; harvesting a slice of 3-5-year-old devices yields supply at ~10-20% of new cost.

title: Open-PDK DRAM foundry with multi-project shuttles on mature lines
idea: Ideal: anyone can make memory. Closest achievable with no new fab: a DRAM maker sells wafer slots on a 2x-nm DRAM line with an open PDK (cell, capacitor, sense-amp library) and quarterly MPW shuttles, so fabless firms build custom wide-I/O, PIM and embedded DRAM.
why: Adds revenue to depreciated lines and unlocks custom architectures that cut data-movement energy.

title: Hatch-Waxman generic-DRAM pathway with bioequivalence-style qualification
idea: Like generic drugs that need only to prove bioequivalence, a second-source maker proves 'JEDEC equivalence' to a reference DDR4/LPDDR4 part on a certified test suite (timing, retention, hammer, thermal) and is then approved by all signatory OEMs without each running full qualification.
why: Lets new and U.S. fabs sell legacy DRAM in months instead of 1-2 years of per-customer qualification, increasing second-source supply.

title: Fab inside the sewage plant: reclaimed effluent as feedwater
idea: Reverse the water source: build the fab next to a municipal wastewater plant and make UPW from tertiary-treated effluent. Concentrated brine goes back to the plant, so the fab draws no potable or fresh water.
why: Fresh-water withdrawal per wafer falls >10x (near zero). Water stops being a siting veto in Arizona- and Texas-type locations.

title: Display-fab memory panels: IGZO gain cells on Gen-8.5 glass
idea: Combine an idle Gen-8.5 oxide-TFT display line (2.2×2.5 m glass) with gain-cell memory arrays. The line patterns low-density IGZO 2T memory tiles in panels, which are diced into large, slow-but-cheap memory slabs for capacity tiers.
why: Display fabs are already-depreciated, sit at about 30% utilization, and cost roughly 1/50 per m² of a DRAM fab. That suits an ultra-low-$/m² capacity tier even at 100× lower density.

title: Noble-gas intensity credit: CHIPS bonus for rare-gas-free fabs
idea: Time-bounded policy: production credits scale with a fab's measured liters of helium, neon, argon and xenon per wafer, falling to zero by 2032, so every procurement decision pushes toward substitute processes.
why: Makes U.S. DRAM capacity immune to the Qatar-style and Ukraine-style gas shocks while sharing the substitution cost. It also builds a U.S. market for the tools in ideas 24-42.

title: DRAM futures exchange to break the boom-bust capex cycle
idea: Reverse when risk is taken: a cleared futures market trades a standard contract (e.g., 1 Tb of DDR5-equivalent delivered per quarter). Fabs sell output 2-3 years forward to finance capex, and buyers hedge price spikes.
why: Capital intensity: forward-sold output lowers financing risk and keeps capex steady through downturns, damping 4x price swings like the current one.

title: Warehouse receipt: exchange-traded DRAM bit futures with bonded physical delivery
idea: Random stimulus 'pawnshop warehouse receipt' -> metals trade on LME warrants. List standardized DDR5 16 Gb component futures, deliverable from bonded warehouses, so producers hedge 3-5 years forward and banks lend against hedged output to finance fabs.
why: Lowers cost of capital for capacity (fact 4: depreciation ~55% of wafer cost) and gives small buyers price certainty; est. 1-3 pts lower WACC on fab debt.

title: Exchange-traded DRAM bit futures for long-dated hedging
idea: Po: bits are traded like wheat. A standardized cash-settled contract (e.g., 1 Tb of DDR5-equivalent per quarter against a published contract-price index) lets fabs sell output 3-5 years forward and buyers hedge, so a greenfield fab can be project-financed against hedged revenue.
why: Hedged revenue opens project finance to new entrants and cuts the risk premium over the 3-5-year build gap; attacks capital intensity.

title: Lorentz-force cold-crucible pulling frees silicon crystals from Spruce Pine quartz
idea: Grow DRAM-grade ingots in a segmented water-cooled copper crucible where induced currents push the melt off the walls (electromagnetic skull melting), so no high-purity quartz crucible touches silicon. Oxygen for intrinsic gettering is dosed back via controlled SiO/O2 gas feed.
why: Eliminates >80% single-site HPQ dependency; quartz crucibles are consumed every pull, so wafer supply decouples from one mine.

title: No silicon wafer: HDD media lines make MRAM crossbars on glass disks
idea: Forced limit: use another industry's substrate and tools. Hard-disk media lines, which sputter thousands of glass platters an hour and nanoimprint bit-patterned media, deposit MTJ plus threshold-selector crossbars on 95 mm glass disks.
why: Capital: reuses a shrinking HDD media industry with world-class sputter and nanoimprint tools, adding non-Si, endurance-unlimited memory capacity.

title: Controller-side line compression licensed per gigabyte saved
idea: Box[Transform=CPU memory-controller LZ-class cache-line compression x Integration=unchanged DDR5 channel x Owner=IP licensor x Finance=royalty per effective GB]: the controller compresses lines into packed physical pages (IBM MXT style) with metadata cache, and the licensor is paid per effective GB delivered.
why: Doing DRAM's job with less: ~1.5-2x effective capacity on typical data; same DIMMs.

title: Triboelectric-tagged module plastics separate cleanly in electrostatic sorters
idea: Mold compound, DIMM PCB resin and heat-spreader coatings get additives that pin each to a distinct place in the triboelectric series. Shredded fragments are tumbled and dropped through a high-voltage free-fall separator into pure streams.
why: Raises recovered-metal and silicon purity above ~95%, so module recycling pays for itself.

title: Glulam lamination: tiny high-yield DRAM tiles bonded on logic
idea: Adapted from glulam beams that laminate small knot-free boards into big members: a young U.S. DUV fab makes 2-4 mm2 DRAM tiles, and only known-good tiles are hybrid-bonded side by side onto a U.S.-made logic base die that carries the periphery.
why: A defect costs one tile instead of a ~70 mm2 die, so yield stays >95% at defect densities that would sink big dies; a new U.S. fab ships sellable bits years earlier on its learning curve (U.S. manufacturability, capital).

title: RAID-style base die makes commodity DRAM 125 C-capable
idea: Like RAID making cheap disks reliable, stack ordinary commodity DRAM die on a logic base die with symbol-level ECC, a per-row refresh map measured at 125 C, and spare-row remapping, so ordinary die meet 10 years at 125 C.
why: Ends the split between commodity and automotive die, so any DRAM wafer can serve either market and supply becomes fungible.

title: HMC's mistake fixed: open multi-vendor base die for HBM stacks
idea: Micron's Hybrid Memory Cube died as a closed consortium product built on a single-vendor logic base die, and it lost to JEDEC HBM. Fix: standardize the core-die-to-base-die interface (TSV map, protocol, test hooks) so any maker's DRAM core dies can be stacked onto any foundry-made base die, and smaller DRAM makers can sell qualified core dies into HBM.
why: HBM TSV tax and supply concentration: widens the pool of HBM core-die suppliers beyond three firms and moves base-die silicon out of scarce DRAM fabs.

title: MRAM finishing micro-fabs adding MTJ stacks to foundry wafers
idea: Worse: require a full front-end fab to make any new memory. Flip: build ~$300-500M back-end-only micro-fabs that take finished CMOS wafers from any foundry, add MTJ stacks between metal layers, and return them.
why: Nonvolatile, so zero refresh; capital roughly 1/20 of a DRAM fab, with manufacturing spread across U.S. sites.

title: Seed bank: strategic reserve of unpackaged known-good DRAM die
idea: Random stimulus 'seed bank' -> vault seeds against famine. A federal reserve buys tested, unpackaged DRAM die in gluts, stores them in dry-N2 vaults (unpowered die do not wear), and releases them to packagers during shortages, sized at ~60 days of critical demand.
why: Counter-cyclical buying smooths the boom-bust capex cycle and caps price spikes like the 4x 2025-26 jump; it protects defense and medical supply.

title: MoSys 1T-SRAM afterlife: hidden-refresh DRAM replaces legacy SDRAM
idea: MoSys's 1T-SRAM (DRAM cells with hidden refresh behind an SRAM interface, built at 180 nm for Nintendo's GameCube) faded as embedded memory moved on. Fix: build standalone 64-512 Mb SRAM-interface DRAM chips on 180 nm, 200 mm lines to replace the SDR/DDR/DDR2 parts that industrial, automotive and defense customers still buy and the big makers are retiring.
why: Supply: moves legacy-part demand off advanced DRAM lines, and the SRAM-like interface avoids requalifying controllers in products with decades-long lives.

title: Dry resist, dry develop: deposit and etch the photoresist
idea: Reverse lithography's wet track: deposit metal-oxide photoresist by vapor and develop it by plasma or thermal dry etch. That eliminates spin coat, aqueous TMAH develop and rinse on every patterned layer.
why: Develop and rinse across 30+ litho layers use a lot of water and chemicals. Dry resist cuts that water ~10x and lowers EUV dose, which stretches scarce EUV capacity.

title: Sculptor carves inside the block: 50 porous-silicon tiers in one wet step
idea: A sculptor carves inside the block instead of adding clay. Pulse the current while anodizing a bulk Si wafer in HF to form 50 alternating high- and low-porosity layers in one ~10-minute wet step. A hydrogen anneal reseals the low-porosity layers into single-crystal Si sheets over voids (silicon-on-nothing physics), giving a 50-tier channel stack without epitaxy.
why: Meets the 10x constraint: a wet electrochemical step costing under ~$50 per wafer replaces a $1,000+ epitaxial superlattice, so a 50-tier 3D DRAM (~10x/mm^2) keeps wafer cost flat. It needs only U.S. wet-bench suppliers and no scarce gases.

title: Strategic DRAM Reserve buying wafers at troughs, releasing at peaks
idea: Worse: let three makers cut capex in sync every bust so the next boom becomes a 4x price spike. Flip: a chartered reserve buys known-good DRAM wafers in price troughs, stores them in nitrogen vaults, and auctions them when contract prices rise more than 50% year on year.
why: Damps the boom-bust cycle, gives fabs a price floor that justifies counter-cyclical capex, and buffers ~3 months of national demand.

title: ISS-style hot-spare dies that auto-swap in the field
idea: Space stations carry spares because resupply is rare. A 10-person team builds modules with one or two spare DRAM packages and a small mux controller that copies a degrading chip's contents and fails over automatically, so a module serves 12-15 years instead of being pulled at its first chip failure.
why: About doubles module service life and cuts replacement demand.

title: Printed-memory failures fixed: oxide-TFT DRAM on retired LCD lines
idea: Printed and plastic memories (Thin Film Electronics, Kovio) died without a dense, fast product. Fix: use retired Gen-2 to Gen-4 LCD lines (1990s tools, 1.5-3 um lithography, sputter tools reused for oxide channels) to make 1T1C DRAM in oxide TFTs on glass, where very low off-current gives minutes of retention, over square meters instead of wafers.
why: Capital and U.S. manufacturability: ~2 GB per m^2 on fully depreciated panel tools, so cost per bit rests on cheap area rather than litho; a refresh-light bulk tier at ~100 ns-1 us.

title: Socket offload: depreciated 200 mm fabs make low-density DRAM
idea: Extreme user: $1 IoT, automotive and industrial sockets need only 64 Mb-4 Gb but draw on the same suppliers' wafer starts. Re-tool shuttered U.S. 200 mm fabs, fully depreciated at ~0.1x capital, with 65-45 nm trench DRAM for these sockets, freeing leading-edge starts for high-density bits.
why: Depreciation is ~55% of wafer cost (fact 4); a paid-off fab serves low-density sockets cheaply and frees leading-edge capacity.

title: Prompt-prefix commons: one shared KV cache per data center
idea: Extreme user: AI KV-cache, where thousands of tenants send identical system prompts and documents. Providers agree on canonical tokenization and keep shared read-only KV pages for common prefixes in a pooled CXL tier, stored once with copy-on-write.
why: Cuts inference DRAM demand 20-50% for chat workloads; usable supply rises with no new bits.

title: VW MQB-style platform die serving DDR5, LPDDR5 and GDDR
idea: Adapted from car platforms that sit under many models: one DRAM core die whose I/O personality (bus width, voltages, PHY) is set by a single late metal layer or by a bonded base chiplet, so a fab can swing wafers among DDR5, LPDDR5 and GDDR in weeks.
why: Shortages are often segment-specific; swingable capacity cuts stranded inventory and mask sets, raising usable supply ~5-10% across the cycle (supply, masks).

title: Fabric-wide content-addressed page dedup across many hosts
idea: Ideal: every unique byte is stored exactly once in the world. Closest achievable: a CXL pool controller hashes 4 KB pages and keeps one copy of duplicates (OS images, libraries, shared model weights, zero pages) across dozens of hosts, with hardware copy-on-write.
why: Usable capacity: 20-40% fewer physical bits in multi-tenant clouds.

title: Refurbished ArF immersion scanners with SAQP for EUV-free DRAM
idea: Box[Fab=secondhand ArFi scanners + self-aligned quadruple patterning x Owner=new-entrant fab x Finance=used-tool leasing]: patterning 1a-class DRAM with refurbished ArFi tools and SAQP instead of EUV lets entrants make DDR5-compliant parts without a single-supplier EUV tool.
why: Capital and chokepoint: avoids EUV single-supplier dependence and cuts litho capex ~50-70% at some cost in steps.

title: EUV-free 1y-class DRAM micro-fab built from refurbished immersion scanners
idea: Derive the cost floor from tool $ per patterned layer: a 6F^2 cell at F~17 nm needs only 193i SAQP, and a refurbished immersion scanner costs ~1/8 of an EUV tool. Build a 10k-wafer/month U.S. line on second-hand 193i, etch and ALD tools running a frozen ~17 nm process, accepting ~50% of leading density at ~25% of capex per wafer start.
why: Capital intensity, EUV chokepoint and U.S. manufacturability: roughly 2x bits per capex dollar versus a leading-edge greenfield, and a 2-3 year ramp with no single-supplier tool.

title: Free-electron-laser EUV utility shared by a cluster of U.S. fabs
idea: An energy-recovery-linac FEL's undulator radiation produces >10 kW at 13.5 nm, enough to feed 8-10 scanners. Build a national-lab-operated light utility on a fab campus that sells photons per joule to tenant fabs, with a beamline interface standard so a second scanner vendor can enter.
why: Cuts EUV source energy and cost per scanner and decouples the source from the single vendor; campus-level capital sharing.

title: Users must hedge the cycle: cash-settled DRAM bit futures
idea: Self-imposed limit: no unhedged exposure. An exchange lists a standardized cash-settled future per Gb of DDR5-equivalent, so buyers lock in prices and makers sell output forward to finance capex years ahead.
why: Capital intensity: forward sales lower the cost of capital and smooth the price spikes that starve investment.

title: Patent-expiry DRAM: open PDK built only from 20-year-old patents
idea: Decade time shift of IP: assemble a full cell, sense-amp and periphery design kit using only techniques from patents that expired more than 20 years ago, then publish it as an open PDK so new U.S. entrants have freedom to operate on day one.
why: Removes the licensing and litigation barrier that keeps entrants out of DRAM. Cuts years of legal risk and IP cost, enabling cooperative or startup fabs.

title: WWII tungsten-to-molybdenum swap using Colorado molybdenum wordlines
idea: Adapted from WWII toolmakers who replaced scarce tungsten with molybdenum M-series high-speed steels: replace W in buried wordlines, contacts and bitline plugs with ALD/CVD Mo. The precursors are synthesized in the U.S. from molybdenum mined in Colorado (Climax/Henderson).
why: Removes the China ~80% tungsten chokepoint with an all-U.S. metal chain; Mo resists better at narrow widths and can run barrier-less, which helps wordline RC (scarce resources, U.S. manufacturability).

title: Sand-to-DRAM county campus with every input sourced domestically
idea: Transport and inventory buffers are pure overhead, so co-locate every abundant-element stage on one site: sand carbochlorination to SiCl4, polysilicon, synthetic-crucible ingots, wafers and an eleven-element DRAM fab, with Al, Ti and Zr precursors from domestic ilmenite and zircon sands. Cascade waste heat from polysilicon reactors into fab HVAC and water recycling.
why: U.S. manufacturability: zero foreign chokepoints for any input; inventory buffers and logistics risk collapse, and shared utilities cut capex.

title: Chlorine-etchable spacer materials for EUV-free quadruple patterning
idea: Combine self-aligned quadruple patterning with spacer and hard-mask materials chosen to etch in BCl3/Cl2 (TiO2, ZrO2, HfO2) on carbon mandrels removed by O2 ash, replacing SiN and SiO2 spacers that need fluorocarbon etchback.
why: Enables F-free pitch division to 12-14 nm half-pitch without EUV, attacking the EUV and capex bottleneck.

title: O: Synthetic sol-gel silica crucibles from polysilicon-plant SiCl4 waste
idea: Hydrolyze the SiCl4 byproduct of Siemens polysilicon plants into ultra-pure sol-gel/fumed silica, slip-cast and arc-fuse it into fully synthetic CZ crucibles (bubble-free inner wall, nucleated outer wall), qualified in a U.S. plant.
why: Breaks the >80% Spruce Pine high-purity-quartz dependence for crucibles while converting a waste stream into feedstock; secures U.S. wafer supply for DRAM.

title: Certified pre-owned RDIMMs with robotic retest and pooled warranty
idea: Box[Source=retired DDR4/DDR5 RDIMMs x Transform=robotic thermal retest + SPD rewrite x Integration=plug-in standard DIMM x Owner=refurbisher x Finance=pooled warranty insurance]: grade decommissioned DIMMs at hot and cold corners, rewrite SPD with remaining-life data, and sell them back into standard DDR slots with an insurer-backed 3-year warranty.
why: Supply from reuse with the interface untouched: an estimated 10%+ of server DIMM demand could be met at ~30-50% of new price.

title: Phone LPDDR harvested and rebuilt into LPCAMM2 modules
idea: Box[Source=retired flagship phones x Transform=separate discrete LPDDR5 packages, reball, retest x Integration=standard LPCAMM2 for laptops and edge servers x Owner=e-waste refurbisher]: billions of phones hold 8-16 GB of LPDDR; recover the discrete packages and assemble them into standard LPCAMM2 modules.
why: Large untapped reuse pool (an estimated multi-EB of LPDDR retired per year) feeding standard LPDDR5 interfaces.

title: Pure-play DRAM foundry for fabless memory designers
idea: Inverts 'whoever designs DRAM must own the fab': a foundry offers a frozen DRAM cell/capacitor platform with an open periphery design kit so fabless firms tape out custom interfaces, logic-in-periphery and niche densities.
why: Supply diversity and utilization: lets startups enter without $15B, keeps the foundry full across cycles, and creates specialty parts that relieve commodity demand.

title: Constraint-tool debottlenecking with refurbished secondary-market tools
idea: Ideal: an existing fab produces 2x with no construction. Closest achievable: simulate each DRAM fab's queue network to find the 2-3 constraint tool groups (often high-AR etch, ALD, ArFi) and fill cleanroom whitespace with refurbished copies of only those tools.
why: Capacity: +8-15% wafer outs at ~5% of greenfield capex per added wafer.

title: Short-retention DRAM bins sold for ephemeral AI data
idea: Po: memory that forgets on purpose. Dies that fail the 64 ms retention screen but pass at 16 or 32 ms are no longer scrapped; they are marked R16/R32 in SPD, priced lower, and paired with controllers that refresh 2-4x faster or host only data that lives <10 ms (activations, KV-cache scratch, network buffers).
why: Retention-tail failures are a major yield-loss bin; recovering them could add several percent sellable bits per wafer at zero capex; attacks cost per bit and supply.

title: Eliminate desoldering: old smartphone boards as ARM microserver nodes
idea: Eliminate extraction of soldered LPDDR entirely: refurbish 4-8GB smartphone logic boards (battery removed, USB-PD power, Ethernet over USB-C) into rack microserver nodes running containerized CI and edge workloads; $1M pilots 5,000 nodes.
why: Reuses DRAM and SoC together, offloading workloads that would otherwise consume new server DRAM.

title: No silicon, no vacuum: EHD-jet printed oxide memory micro-fabs
idea: Forced limit: no wafer, no vacuum fab. Electrohydrodynamic jet printers write solution-processed ZTO/IGZO and metal lines at about 1 um on glass sheets in $5M micro-fabs distributed near users.
why: Distributed manufacturing: capital per site drops by about 1000x, giving local supply for defense and edge niches; density is low.

title: Cleanroom REIT: separate fab shells from tool capital
idea: Reverse the capital stack: a real-estate investment trust builds and owns the cleanroom shells, utilities, UPW and power plants. It leases them on 20-year terms to DRAM operators, who buy only tools.
why: Capital intensity: the shell and facilities are ~20-30% of fab cost. Financing them at REIT cost of capital (~6-8%) instead of chipmaker equity (~12%+) lowers the depreciation and finance charge per wafer.

title: Tradable 10-year bit-futures that securitize new fab output
idea: Financial time shift: hyperscalers and OEMs buy standardized forward contracts for Gb delivered in years 4-10 of a planned fab. The contracts trade on an exchange, and a fab SPV issues bonds against them, so the $15B build is funded by demand that is already committed.
why: Attacks capital intensity and the 3-5 year build risk. Cost of capital falls perhaps 300-500 bp, worth ~5-8% on cost per bit, since depreciation is ~55% of wafer cost.

title: Wet-activated hybrid bonding for HBM stacks without argon beams
idea: Molecular-scale surface engineering: activate copper and oxide bond pads with a dilute chemical bath and water-vapor plasma instead of the argon fast-atom beams used for surface-activated bonding, then bond at room temperature.
why: Stacking 8-16 HBM dies multiplies argon-intensive activation steps. Wet activation makes the HBM back end rare-gas-free and cheaper per stack.
